steps.title: Import TypeScript type utilities
steps.instruction: Add an import statement at the top of your file to bring in TypeScript's built-in type utilities that we'll use as building blocks.
steps.hint: TypeScript doesn't require explicit imports for its built-in type utilities like keyof and generics - they're available globally. Just create a basic TypeScript file structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a basic TypeScript file ready to implement the ValueOf type.
successCriteria: The file contains valid TypeScript syntax and is ready for implementing type utilities.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up your TypeScript file correctly. TypeScript's built-in type utilities like keyof and generics are available globally, so no explicit imports are needed.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Remember that TypeScript's core type utilities are built-in and don't require imports. Just ensure you have valid TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. TypeScript doesn't need explicit imports for its built-in type utilities. Just create a basic TypeScript file structure.

steps.title: Create the ValueOf type definition
steps.instruction: Define a generic type named ValueOf that takes a single type parameter T.
steps.hint: Start with 'type ValueOf<T> = ' and think about what you want to extract from T.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a generic type that extracts keys
type KeysOf<T> = keyof T;
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a generic type definition ready to be implemented.
successCriteria: A generic type named ValueOf with a single type parameter T is defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the ValueOf type with a generic parameter.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're defining a type named ValueOf with a generic parameter T.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to define a generic type named ValueOf with one type parameter.

steps.title: Add the keyof constraint to ValueOf
steps.instruction: Modify the ValueOf type definition to constrain its generic parameter T to be an object by adding `extends object` after the type parameter.
steps.hint: Add `extends object` after the generic type parameter T to restrict it to object types only.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: constraining a generic to an object type
type ExtractKeys<T extends object> = keyof T;
steps.seedCode:
// Add your TypeScript code here
type ValueOf<T> = T[keyof T];
steps.expectedOutcome: The ValueOf type will now only accept object types for its generic parameter T.
successCriteria: The ValueOf type definition includes `extends object` constraint on the generic parameter T.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully constrained the ValueOf type to work only with object types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added `extends object` after the type parameter T in the ValueOf definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constraint is missing. Add `extends object` after the generic type parameter T to restrict it to object types.

steps.title: Implement the indexed access type
steps.instruction: Test your ValueOf type by creating a sample interface and using it to extract a property value type.
steps.hint: Create an interface with some properties, then use ValueOf<YourInterface> to get the type of one of its properties.
steps.seedCode:
type ValueOf<T> = T[keyof T];

// Test the ValueOf type by creating an interface and using it
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll verify that ValueOf correctly extracts property value types from an interface.
successCriteria: An interface is created with at least two properties, and ValueOf is used to extract the type of one property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully tested the ValueOf type with a concrete interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you create an interface and use ValueOf<YourInterface> to extract a property type.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the expected implementation. Review how indexed access types work.

steps.title: Create a test object type
steps.instruction: Define an interface named 'User' with three properties: 'id' (number), 'name' (string), and 'email' (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a User interface with typed properties ready to test the ValueOf utility.
successCriteria: The User interface is defined with id: number, name: string, and email: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the User interface with the correct property types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your User interface has exactly three properties: id (number), name (string), and email (string).
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the requirement. Define an interface named User with id: number, name: string, and email: string properties.

steps.title: Test ValueOf with string properties
steps.instruction: Inside your User interface, add a property called 'name' with type 'string' and another property called 'email' with type 'string'.
steps.hint: Add two string properties to the User interface: name and email. This will allow you to test ValueOf with string value types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The User interface will have two string properties: name and email, which you can later use to test the ValueOf type.
successCriteria: The User interface contains both 'name: string' and 'email: string' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added string properties to the User interface. These will be used to test how ValueOf extracts string value types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some properties, but make sure you have both 'name: string' and 'email: string' in the User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface should contain two string properties: 'name' and 'email'. Try adding them inside the interface body.

steps.title: Test ValueOf with number properties
steps.instruction: Add a 'age' property with type number to the User interface.
steps.hint: Add a property named 'age' with the type annotation ': number' inside the User interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The User interface will have a number property, allowing you to test ValueOf with number types in the next step.
successCriteria: The User interface includes a property named 'age' with type 'number'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a number property to the User interface. This will let us test how ValueOf works with number types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a property named 'age' with the type 'number' inside the User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on this step: add a property called 'age' with type 'number' to the User interface.

steps.title: Test ValueOf with boolean properties
steps.instruction: Add a boolean property named 'isActive' to the User interface.
steps.hint: Inside the User interface, add a property with the name 'isActive' and type it as 'boolean'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The User interface now includes a boolean property, allowing you to test ValueOf with boolean types.
successCriteria: The User interface has a property named 'isActive' with type 'boolean'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a boolean property to the User interface. This will let us test how ValueOf handles boolean types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a property named 'isActive' with the type 'boolean' inside the User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface doesn't have a boolean property named 'isActive'. Add 'isActive: boolean;' inside the interface.

steps.title: Create a function using ValueOf
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'logUserProperty' that accepts a parameter of type 'ValueOf<User>' and returns void. Inside the function, log the parameter to the console.
steps.hint: Define a function with the signature (property: ValueOf<User>): void. Use console.log inside the function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named logUserProperty is created that accepts a ValueOf<User> parameter and logs it.
successCriteria: The logUserProperty function is defined with proper TypeScript syntax, accepts a ValueOf<User> parameter, and logs it to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a function that uses the ValueOf type. This demonstrates how ValueOf can be applied in practical scenarios like function parameters.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function accepts a parameter of type ValueOf<User> and logs it to the console. Check the function name and return type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Remember to define a function named logUserProperty that takes a ValueOf<User> parameter and logs it.

steps.title: Test the function with different values
steps.instruction: Call your logUserProperty function three times: once with a string value, once with a number value, and once with a boolean value.
steps.hint: Use the function name followed by parentheses and pass appropriate arguments that match the User interface property types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should be called with three different values that correspond to the property types in the User interface.
successCriteria: logUserProperty is called three times with arguments of type string, number, and boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully tested the ValueOf type by calling the function with values that match the User property types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've called the function, but make sure you call it three times with values of each type: string, number, and boolean.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function calls are missing or incorrect. Call logUserProperty three times with appropriate values.
